Component 03 · Weeks 12–15

Robotic Drawing and Material Exploration

What changes when a machine follows the same path with a different tool? In Weeks 12–15, students revisit three Recreate the Past studies through pencil plots and material trials, then use one selected sketch to make a series of physical drawings.

Two details from Liat Grayver with e-David, Six Variations on Gestural Computer-Generated Brushstrokes, 2016. Photo © Marcus Nebe. View the series ↓

Lecture overview

Path and mark

The SVG describes where the tool travels. Contact with paper gives the line its width, edge and texture.

Tool and contact

Compare a pen tip with a flexible brush. Look at what happens when a stroke begins, turns and lifts.

Paint and surface

Watch how paint load, dilution and paper absorbency affect opacity, pooling and broken edges.

Repeat to compare

Hold the path and scale steady when comparing materials. A trial can also reveal where the linework needs revision.

Materiality in robotic drawing

A path painted six ways

In Six Variations on Gestural Computer-Generated Brushstrokes, Liat Grayver and the e-David team repeated a generated path at the same speed. Brushes, paint consistency and reloading changed across the series. Follow the loops across all six canvases and notice where the paint covers, thins or breaks.

Pen and brush on one sheet

Roman Verostko used ink pens and a Chinese brush mounted in the drawing arm of a pen plotter. In Untitled #81, the pens build a fine, coloured field. The brush leaves thick, uneven black gestures across it. Look at how the difference in line weight separates the gestures from the background.

Wet paint follows the brush

In Layers 01, Florian Markus places the acrylic paint and the robot moves the brush. The repeated turns give the work its rhythm. Where the brush pulls neighbouring colours together, they blend along the stroke. The close-up shows paint building up at the turns and leaving ridges on the canvas.

Little Drawing Machine: Exploring Robotic and Material Execution

Final project · 30 points · Introduced Week 12 · Due Week 15

  1. Part 1 — Material Exploration of Robotic Drawing

    Weeks 12–13

    Choose three of the six Recreate the Past studies and start from your own p5.js sketch for each. Complete Round A and Round B for each sketch, for at least six explorations.

    Begin each round with a pencil plot to check the path. Then test tools, colour or paint, and paper. For Round B, choose a different material or combination and start again with a pencil plot. If you change parameters, save the earlier sketch and plot the revised version for comparison.

    Record the pencil plots, key trials and selected results with their materials and sketch versions. Include failed or unexpected trials that helped you decide what to change.

  2. Part 2 — Material Showcase of Robotic Drawing

    Weeks 14–15

    Select one saved sketch version from Part 1 and export one SVG. Use that same file at the same scale for every work. Make at least three physical variations using different material combinations and mount each one.

  3. Week 15 submission

    Upload one PDF documenting both parts, including photographs of the mounted series and of each work, and one shared SVG. Bring at least three mounted artworks to class.

Preparing the file for the plotter

Use portrait A3 (297 × 420 mm) with at least 30 mm clear on each edge. Preserve proportions and check the SVG’s physical dimensions and full path bounds, allowing for the widest mark. Test the tool fit and clearance on a small sample before a full drawing.

Material tests

Keep the path and scale fixed for each comparison. Label the material you changed and look at where the difference shows up.

ChangeCompareLook for
Pen typeFineliner and felt tip on the same paperLine width, sharpness at turns and whether gaps stay open
Brush shapeRound and flat brushes with the same paint and paperHow the edge and width change as the tool turns
Paint loadTwo paint loads with the same brush and paperWhere paint pools, thins or runs dry
PaperThe same tool and medium on two paper stocksFeathering, broken edges and the visibility of the paper grain
